reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Metabolic alkalosis is a primary rise in serum bicarbonate with a compensatory increase in carbon dioxide from reduced ventilation
Understanding it requires separating the process that generates the alkalosis from the factors that allow the kidney to maintain it
Urine chloride is the single most useful test for classification, dividing cases into chloride-responsive (low urine chloride) and chloride-resistant (high urine chloride) forms
Chloride-responsive alkalosis, from vomiting, nasogastric suction, or diuretics, is accompanied by volume and chloride depletion and corrects with saline and potassium repletion
Chloride-resistant alkalosis reflects mineralocorticoid excess or severe potassium depletion and does not respond to saline, so the underlying disorder must be treated
Hypokalaemia both contributes to and is worsened by alkalosis, and the two often need correcting together
Maintenance of the alkalosis depends on factors such as volume contraction, chloride depletion, potassium depletion, and mineralocorticoid activity that impair renal bicarbonate excretion
Severe alkalaemia can cause neuromuscular irritability, arrhythmias, and reduced tissue oxygen delivery, and may need more aggressive correction
reference.pathophysiology: Metabolic alkalosis arises when there is a net gain of bicarbonate or a loss of hydrogen ions, but its persistence depends on the kidney's inability to excrete the excess bicarbonate. Normally the kidney can excrete a large bicarbonate load rapidly, so an alkalosis is only sustained when a maintenance factor is present. Generation occurs through loss of acid from the upper gastrointestinal tract or the kidney, or from a gain of alkali. Maintenance results from conditions that increase renal bicarbonate reabsorption, including reduced effective circulating volume, chloride depletion, potassium depletion, and excess mineralocorticoid activity, all of which enhance sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption and hydrogen secretion. In chloride-responsive states, volume and chloride depletion drive the maintenance and are corrected by saline; in chloride-resistant states, ongoing mineralocorticoid excess or profound potassium loss sustains the alkalosis despite adequate volume.
additionalDifferentials: Primary hyperaldosteronism and other mineralocorticoid excess states
Milk-alkali syndrome or excessive alkali administration
additionalInvestigations: Arterial or venous blood gas with serum bicarbonate to confirm the primary alkalosis and assess compensation
Serum electrolytes including potassium, chloride, and magnesium
Urine chloride to classify chloride-responsive versus chloride-resistant disease
Assessment of volume status and blood pressure
Plasma renin and aldosterone when a mineralocorticoid cause is suspected
Review of medications and history for vomiting, diuretic, or laxative use
redFlags: Severe alkalaemia causing tetany, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmia
Profound hypokalaemia with muscle weakness or arrhythmia risk
Marked volume depletion with haemodynamic compromise
Hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis suggesting mineralocorticoid excess
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve readily once the generating cause is removed and the maintenance factors (volume, chloride, and potassium depletion) are corrected. Chloride-resistant forms require treatment of the underlying disorder and may persist otherwise. Severe alkalaemia is dangerous but usually reversible with appropriate management, and overall outcome is governed by the underlying condition.
pitfalls: Giving saline to a chloride-resistant alkalosis that will not respond
Failing to measure urine chloride and thereby misclassifying the disorder
Neglecting concurrent potassium and magnesium deficits that perpetuate the alkalosis
Overlooking surreptitious vomiting or diuretic use as the underlying cause
management: Identify and remove the generating cause, stopping loop or thiazide diuretics and controlling vomiting or nasogastric losses with antiemetics and acid-suppression
Correct chloride-responsive disease by restoring volume and chloride with sodium chloride solution alongside potassium chloride repletion
Replace potassium and magnesium, as hypokalaemia both drives and worsens the alkalosis
Treat chloride-resistant disease by addressing the underlying mineralocorticoid excess, using an aldosterone antagonist or definitive management of an adrenal source
Use the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acetazolamide in selected volume-overloaded patients in whom saline loading is undesirable
Reserve haemodialysis or dilute hydrochloric acid infusion for severe alkalaemia with renal impairment unresponsive to other measures
Monitor blood gases and electrolytes, watching for arrhythmia and compensatory hypoventilation
